completed: Notes sync resilience: initSync now detects local-only notes (created while offline or not yet pushed) and auto-pushes them on reconnect. Sync indicator now shows live note count for at-a-glance reassurance.
learned: Offline-first sync has two failure modes worth distinguishing: silent failed pushes (red-dot visible, user can retry) and orphan writes (note exists locally but never made it to the remote). The orphan case is the dangerous one — it looks synced because there's nothing to retry. Detecting it requires comparing local IDs against remote IDs on every init, not just tracking push failures.
session_note: Verified notes persistence by pulling the live /api/gist endpoint — found all notes intact plus 3 commits of gist version history (GitHub retains every prior state of the gist indefinitely, so even corruption is undoable). Confirmed Gist backend is fine to keep long-term with a no-expiration token; KV migration deferred as unnecessary.
aha: Orphan writes are the dangerous failure mode — failed pushes are loud, orphans are silent
struggle: Sketching the failure modes carefully enough to see the orphan case wasn't symmetric to the failed-push case
curiosity_trail: Should other localStorage-first features (theme, filter state) get the same orphan check?

completed: Defensive NaN guard in staleInfo — tracker cards now show 'Bad date format' instead of 'NaN weeks ago · stale' when a tracker's updated field can't be parsed. Diagnosed and provided fix prompts for wild-stewart-homeschool (wrong date format) and garden-app (flat priorities array instead of columns schema). Both repos confirmed fixed by Chad.
learned: JavaScript's new Date() silently returns Invalid Date on unrecognized formats — arithmetic on it produces NaN, not an error, so it can propagate deep into render logic before surfacing. Always isNaN-guard any computed value derived from a user-supplied date string. The second lesson: cross-repo tracker format drift is a real maintenance hazard when the schema lives in each repo independently — worth documenting the exact expected structure clearly so onboarding a new repo is one prompt, not trial and error.
session_note: Both bugs surfaced from Chad looking at the live dashboard. The NaN label was a defensive fix here; the actual tracker corrections happened in the respective repos via Claude Code sessions. Pattern: dashboard catches the symptom, targeted prompts fix the source.
frustration_peak: Two cards on the live dashboard both reading 'NaN weeks ago · stale' at the same time
curiosity_trail: Should the tracker schema be a published JSON schema, validated on read?

learned: Quadratic Bezier curves can be rasterized to PNG with pure stdlib Python by sampling the curve into polygon points and using ray-casting point-in-polygon — no PIL needed even for organic shapes. Three trees identified separately (vs blending into one shrub) needs both shape gaps AND tonal variation; one without the other isn't enough. The chip-syncs-composer pattern is a 'one element, two affordances' UI win — same control answers both 'show me X' and 'I want to add to X'. Naming carries weight: 'Garden' had the right metaphor but conflicted with another project; 'der Hain' (a grove) keeps the metaphor while signalling specificity. The lowercase German article 'der' next to capitalized 'Hain' makes the typography work — article reads as prefix, name stands as the proper noun.
session_note: Chad caught the favicon v1 looking like a shrub instead of three trees. Fix was structural (gaps + trunks) plus tonal (three different green tones), not just one or the other. Cloudflare deployment loop (push to main → live) makes visual iteration like this practical.
aha: Three trees needs structural gaps AND tonal variation — neither alone is enough

completed: iOS companion app skeleton scaffolded in ios/ subfolder — DerHain (WKWebView wrapper, full-screen, pull-to-refresh, external links route to Safari, dashboard stays in-app) + DerHainWidget (home screen widget, small + medium, fetches projects.json then top tracker priority via GitHub Contents API, refreshes 45min). SETUP.md walkthrough for Xcode project creation, target wiring, and wired-deploy to personal iPhone (no App Store, no TestFlight). CLAUDE.md updated with widget-schema-sync maintenance rule and iOS scope reflected in Out of Scope table.
learned: A WKWebView wrapper is the right intermediate step between PWA and full native rewrite — 95% of features stay web (auto-update on Cloudflare deploy, single codebase) while iOS-only platform integrations (widgets, Action Button, Keychain, native haptics) get added incrementally as native code only when they pay off. The widget extension is a separate target with its own bundle identifier and can't share code with the WebView app directly — it parses tracker JSON itself, so any schema change is a manual sync point. WKWebView's localStorage is isolated from Safari's, so PWA-installed users get a 'first launch' moment where the Gist sync rehydrates their notes. .xcodeproj files contain user-specific UUIDs and signing config — better to leave them out of git and have setup instructions reproduce them locally.
session_note: Chad isn't at his Mac, so all Swift was written 'cold' and committed; he'll open Xcode later and run through ios/SETUP.md. This is the first Swift code in the project-dashboard repo — first dual-platform project he's structured this way. The 'thin wrapper, web is source of truth' pattern is the explicit architectural commitment — keeps maintenance burden low while still unlocking iOS-only surfaces.
aha: WKWebView wrapper is the right intermediate step — keeps web as source of truth while unlocking iOS-only surfaces
wonder: Widget extensions are isolated processes with their own bundle ID — they really can't import from the main app's code, even if they're in the same Xcode project.
first_ever: First Swift code in this repo
